title: State v. Marcus Hale
summary: A night-time burglary of an electronics shop. The accused was stopped two hours later with boxed laptops in his car.
jurisdictionNote: Training case set in a fictional common-law jurisdiction. Names, events and rules are invented for instruction and are not legal advice.

defendant.name: Marcus Hale
defendant.background: Part-time warehouse worker who lives with his mother at the same address he has had for nine years.

facts.text: At 02:10 the alarm at Brightline Electronics sounded. The rear door had been forced and six laptops worth about 4,200 in total were missing.
At 04:05 police stopped Hale's car for a broken tail light, two kilometres from the shop. Five boxed laptops matching the stolen stock were on the back seat.
Hale told officers a friend had asked him to store the boxes and declined to answer further questions.
Hale has one previous conviction, for shoplifting groceries three years ago, which was dealt with by a fine. He paid it and has never missed a court date.

Store CCTV shows a hooded figure of similar build forcing the rear door. The footage was exported by the store manager to a USB drive, which sat in his desk for five days before police collected it. The original recording is still on the store's recorder and its hash matches the exported file.
Before trial Hale pleaded guilty to burglary at the first opportunity. Five of the six laptops were recovered undamaged. He has offered to pay for the missing one and for the door.

exhibits.title: CCTV recording, Brightline Electronics rear entrance
exhibits.description: Four minutes of footage from 02:06 to 02:10 showing a hooded figure forcing the rear door and carrying boxes to a car park.
exhibits.provenance: Exported by the store manager to a USB drive the morning after the burglary. The drive stayed in the manager's unlocked desk for five days before police collected it. A forensic examiner confirmed that the export's hash matches the original file, which is still on the store's recorder.
exhibits.objection: The defence says the five days without police custody breaks the chain of custody, so the footage cannot be relied on and must be excluded.

decisionPoints.title: Bail application
decisionPoints.prompt: Hale applies for bail pending trial. The prosecution does not oppose release, but asks for conditions.

submissions.prosecution: The case is strong and the goods were found in his car. We ask for a curfew, residence at his mother's address and no contact with the store or its staff.
submissions.defence: He has lived at the same address for nine years, works, and has never failed to appear. Conditions are unnecessary; he should be released unconditionally.

factors.text: Stable address for nine years and current employment.
One minor previous conviction; no history of failing to appear or of breaching orders.
The alleged offence is non-violent property crime.
The prosecution case is strong: the goods were found in his car.
The accused is presumed entitled to release unless there is a real risk of absconding, reoffending or interfering with witnesses that conditions cannot manage.
He declined to answer questions after his initial explanation.

options.label: Release without conditions
options.feedback: Lawful and close to the mark, but it leaves no protection for the store, which is a direct witness, and it overlooks the strength of the evidence. A light set of conditions fits better.

options.label: Release with a curfew, residence and no-contact conditions
options.feedback: The presumption of release applies, and the modest risks (a strong case and a commercial witness) are fully managed by light conditions.

options.label: Refuse bail and remand in custody
options.feedback: There is no real risk of absconding or reoffending that conditions cannot manage. Custody here is disproportionate for non-violent property crime.

advice.rationale: I would release Mr Hale on conditions. He has lived at the same address for nine years, works, and has never missed a court date, so the presumption of release clearly applies. The evidence against him is strong and the store is a witness, so a curfew, a residence condition and no contact with the store manage those modest risks without custody.

I would remand Mr Hale in custody. His record shows he has failed to appear before, so there is a real risk he will not attend trial. Given the strength of the case against him, he has every incentive to abscond.
advice.flawExplanation: The record shows the opposite: Hale paid his only fine and has never missed a court date (F4). The advice invents a failure to appear and builds the whole case for custody on it.

advice.rationale: I would refuse bail. Mr Hale gave an implausible account and then refused to answer police questions, which suggests he has something to hide and is unlikely to cooperate with the court. That refusal tips the balance toward custody.
advice.flawExplanation: An accused's choice to stay silent is not evidence of risk and cannot count against bail. Without it, nothing suggests a risk that conditions cannot manage.

decisionPoints.title: Admissibility of the CCTV recording
decisionPoints.prompt: The prosecution tenders exhibit P-1. The defence objects that the five-day gap before police collected the USB drive breaks the chain of custody.

submissions.prosecution: The original recording is preserved and the export's hash matches it exactly. The gap goes to weight, not admissibility.
submissions.defence: For five days anyone could have accessed that drive. A broken chain of custody means the footage cannot be trusted and must be excluded.

factors.text: A forensic examiner confirmed the export's hash matches the original recording.
The original recording is still on the store's recorder and available to the defence.
The USB drive spent five days in an unlocked desk before police collected it.
Gaps in the chain of custody usually go to the weight of evidence, not its admissibility, where authenticity is otherwise shown.
The footage is directly relevant to who forced the door.

options.label: Admit the recording
options.feedback: Authenticity is shown independently by the matching hash and the preserved original. The custody gap goes to weight, which the defence can explore in cross-examination.

options.label: Admit with a direction to treat it with caution
options.feedback: Admitting it is right. A caution direction is harmless but unnecessary, because the hash match removes the real concern about tampering.

options.label: Exclude the recording
options.feedback: Exclusion treats an imperfect chain of custody as fatal, even though authenticity is proved another way. That is not the test.

advice.rationale: I would admit the recording. The five-day gap is a fair point for cross-examination, but authenticity is established independently: the export's hash matches the original, which is still on the store's recorder. Gaps like this go to weight rather than admissibility.

I would exclude the recording. The prosecution must show an unbroken chain of custody from collection to court, and five days in an unlocked desk is a clear break. Once the chain is broken, the exhibit is inadmissible.
advice.flawExplanation: There is no rule that an unbroken chain is a precondition of admissibility. The question is whether the exhibit is shown to be what it claims to be, and here the matching hash proves that. Gaps go to weight.

advice.rationale: I would exclude the recording. The drive sat in an unlocked desk for five days with no record of who accessed it, so the court cannot be confident that the footage has not been altered. The risk of unfair prejudice outweighs its value.
advice.flawExplanation: The advice ignores the forensic hash match and the preserved original (F5), which together answer the tampering concern completely.

decisionPoints.title: Sentence
decisionPoints.prompt: Hale has pleaded guilty to burglary of commercial premises. The sentencing range runs from a community order to three years' custody.

submissions.prosecution: This was a planned night-time burglary of a business. We leave the sentence to the court but note his previous conviction.
submissions.defence: He pleaded at the first opportunity, five of the six laptops were recovered, he has offered full compensation, and he is 24 with a stable home and job.

factors.text: Guilty plea at the first opportunity, which attracts the maximum reduction.
Five of six laptops recovered undamaged; compensation offered for the rest and the door.
One previous conviction, for shoplifting groceries, dealt with by a fine.
A deliberate night-time entry into commercial premises by forcing the door.

options.label: Community order with unpaid work and compensation
options.feedback: The early plea, the recovery of the goods, his offer to compensate and his minor record bring this below the custody threshold. A demanding community order meets the purposes of sentencing.

options.label: Short custodial sentence
options.feedback: Arguable for a planned burglary, but it gives too little weight to the early plea, the recovered goods and the offered compensation.

options.label: Custody toward the top of the range
options.feedback: The upper range is for repeat or aggravated burglaries. Nothing here puts the case there.

advice.rationale: I would impose a community order with unpaid work and compensation. The burglary was planned, but Mr Hale pleaded guilty at the first opportunity, almost all the goods were recovered, and he has offered to pay for the rest. With only a minor previous fine, this falls below the custody threshold.

I would impose a short custodial sentence. This was a deliberate night-time break-in at a business, and he has a previous conviction for dishonesty. Recovering the goods does not change the planning involved, so custody is needed to mark its seriousness.
advice.flawExplanation: The advice never accounts for the guilty plea at the first opportunity (F6), which carries the largest available reduction and is what takes the case below the custody threshold.

advice.rationale: I would sentence toward the top of the range. Mr Hale already has a burglary conviction, so this is a repeat offence of the same kind, and repeat burglary of commercial premises calls for a substantial custodial term despite the plea.
advice.flawExplanation: His previous conviction is for shoplifting groceries, dealt with by a fine (F4), not burglary. The advice treats it as a repeat burglary, which inflates the sentence.
